landscape: Political economy draws on a large and heterogeneous body of data. At its centre are official statistics: the World Bank's World Development Indicators, the IMF's World Economic Outlook and data portal, and the OECD, Eurostat, UN and ILO databases. These supply national accounts, prices, trade, public finance and labour series that most cross-national studies use as controls or outcomes. Academic projects rebuild these series for comparison over long periods. The Penn World Table covers real output at purchasing power parity, and the Maddison Project and the Global Macro Database cover long-run growth. Clio Infra, Jordà-Schularick-Taylor and the IMF historical public finance databases cover the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

A second layer consists of datasets built by political scientists and economists to measure institutions and policies. They cover tax revenue (UNU-WIDER GRD, now succeeded by the IMF WoRLD database, and Financing the State), central bank independence, capital controls and exchange rate regimes. Others cover welfare effort and entitlements (OECD SOCX, CWED, CPDS), labour institutions (ICTWSS), economic freedom and regulation, trade policy (Global Trade Alert, tariff databases) and natural resources. Inequality data form a field of their own: SWIID, the World Inequality Database, LIS, WIID and the World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform take different approaches to comparability.

Of the 162 PE rows, 119 are research datasets, 27 data portals and 16 commercial products (financial databases such as Datastream, Bloomberg, Compustat and Orbis, used for work on firms and markets). Several important series changed status recently: the IMF retired International Financial Statistics as a single dataset in 2025, the GRD was frozen in 2025, Doing Business was replaced by B-READY, and the Resource Governance Index was superseded by the Resource Governance Assessment. Many official sites (IMF, OECD, ILO) block automated access, so a number of rows were verified through APIs, metadata or manual browser checks.

core.text: The World Development Indicators are the World Bank's main compilation of development statistics: about 1,400 to 1,600 indicators for 217 economies and regional groups from 1960, covering national accounts, poverty, health, education, environment and governance-related series. They are a common source of control variables in cross-national research and can be accessed through an API and R and Stata packages. Many series are compiled from other agencies, values change between vintages, and modelled estimates are mixed with observed data, so replications should record the download date.

The Penn World Table (version 11.0, 2025) provides real GDP, capital, productivity and prices for 185 countries from 1950 to 2023. It is built on International Comparison Program price benchmarks so that output can be compared across countries at purchasing power parity. It is widely used for growth and development comparisons. Revisions between versions can be large for some economies, and version 11.0 changes the treatment of China, so results should name the release used.

The Maddison Project Database (2023 release) gives GDP per capita and population for 169 countries, with estimates reaching back to antiquity for some and dense annual coverage for the last two centuries. It is widely used for long-run growth and for historical controls in studies of institutions and development. Early estimates are sparse and conjectural, and level comparisons depend on the benchmark year chosen.

The Standardized World Income Inequality Database (version 9.92, 2026) estimates Gini coefficients of disposable and market income for 199 countries from 1960. It uses a Bayesian model to make figures from many sources comparable and distributes the estimates as multiple imputations, which gives it broad comparable coverage. Many country-years rest on imputation, and critics such as Jenkins (2015) have questioned the approach. Analyses should use the imputations rather than point estimates.

The Comparative Political Data Set covers 36 democratic OECD and EU countries from 1960 to 2023, combining political variables (government composition, elections, institutions) with economic, fiscal and social indicators drawn from OECD and other sources. It is widely used in comparative welfare-state and partisan-politics research on rich democracies. Its socio-economic variables are copies of other sources and can lag them, and it does not cover countries outside the OECD and EU.

choosing: Separate the concept from the source. For output and prices, choose by period and comparison: WDI or WEO for recent panels, PWT for real comparisons across countries, Maddison or the Global Macro Database for long-run series. For inequality, choose between survey-based and tax-based measures before choosing a dataset, and never mix income and consumption Gini values.

For institutional measures (central bank independence, capital controls, economic freedom, regulation), results often depend on the indicator chosen. Check robustness across at least two measures, prefer components to composite scores, and record the release used, since most of these indices are re-estimated or re-weighted between editions.
gaps: Fiscal and revenue data for low-income countries before 1980 remain thin; historical tax datasets cover mainly Europe and the Americas, and the GRD has been frozen since 2025.

Comparable data on business associations, lobbying by firms outside the United States, and political connections of firms are scarce; the main cross-national connection dataset (Faccio) is frozen, and a planned global dataset has not been released.

Several standard indices have ended or changed recently (IMF IFS, Doing Business, the Resource Governance Index, the World Bank Privatization Database), and these changes create series breaks. Official IMF, OECD and ILO pages also block automated access, which complicates verification and reproducible downloads.
